Working with Files

Learn to open files safely, pick the correct mode, read and write text, and handle common errors so your programs preserve data reliably.

In this lesson
Open files, read lines, write safely, and use context managers to close files reliably.
Why it matters
File I/O makes programs durable: logs, configuration, and exported data all depend on correct file handling.
Concept Map
open()
Returns a file object and uses a mode string.
Read & Write
read(), readline(), write(), writelines(), and iterating lines.
Context Managers
Use with to auto-close and avoid leaks.
Visual Overview
File lifecycle
Open & Choose Mode
Pick 'r', 'w', 'a', or 'x' depending on whether you need to read, overwrite, append, or create exclusively.
Operate
Read with read/readline or write with write/writelines. Iterate directly for memory-efficient reads.
Explore Key Topics
Open & Modes — Choosing 'r', 'w', 'a', 'x' affects whether you risk truncating files.
Reading Methods — read for small files, iterate for large files to limit memory use.
With statement — ensures files close even when errors occur, preventing resource leaks.

screens.title: Open a file with open()
screens.narratorSegment: When you call the open function you receive a file object: a Python handle that represents an interaction channel with disk storage. That object exposes methods like read, write, and close. Understanding that a file object is a resource explains why you must close it: the operating system allocates buffers and locks on your behalf, and those resources should be released when you’re done. A common misconception is that closing is optional because the interpreter will eventually clean up; while cleanup happens at program end, relying on it can lead to lost data or too many open handles in long-running programs. Use the file object to call read-based methods when you need input, or write-based methods to send text to disk. The file object also maintains the file pointer position; after reading or writing, subsequent operations continue from the pointer. Knowing this helps reason about why mixing read and write calls without adjusting the pointer can produce unexpected results. As a concrete example, opening a file in default mode returns a readable file object you can iterate over. The key takeaway: treat the file object as a resource you open, use, and reliably close.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: open() returns a file object — a resource that you must manage to avoid leaks and data loss.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › Open a file
Core Concept

What open() gives you

A file object with methods and a pointer. It represents the program's access to a file on disk and must be closed when finished.

Key properties
  • Exposes read, write, readline, readlines, and close.
  • Keeps a current position pointer used by sequential operations.
  • Is a resource allocated by the OS that needs release.
Key Takeaway

Treat file objects as managed resources: open, use, and close to avoid leaks and unfinished writes.

Concrete example
# Open a file for reading
file = open("my_data.txt", "r")
content = file.read()
print(content)
file.close()

# File object methods: read(), readline(), write(), close()
Misconception
Relying on program exit to close files risks lost buffered writes during long-running processes.
Pro tip
Prefer the with statement to ensure closure even if exceptions occur.

screens.title: File modes: 'r', 'w', 'a', and 'x'
screens.narratorSegment: File modes determine whether you can read, write, or append and whether a file is created or truncated. The default 'r' opens an existing file for reading and raises an error if it does not exist. 'w' opens for writing and will create a file if needed but will also truncate an existing file to zero length — this is why using 'w' when you intended to append causes accidental data loss. 'a' opens the file for appending: writes are added to the end and the file is created if missing, making it the safe choice for log entries. 'x' tries to create the file and fails with an exception if the file already exists; this is useful when you want exclusive creation. A common beginner mistake is using 'w' for repeated updates. For example, appending a log entry should use 'a', not 'w'. Another consideration is that modes can include a 'b' for binary; in this chapter we focus on text files, so use the default text mode. Always double-check the chosen mode to avoid losing content, and prefer explicit choices: if you need to preserve content, use 'a' or open and read-then-write with care.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › File modes
Comparison

File modes at a glance

'r' — Read
Requires existing file, returns content for reading. Raises FileNotFoundError if missing.
'w' — Write
Creates or truncates file. Use when you intentionally overwrite content.
'a' — Append
Creates if missing and writes at end. Ideal for logs where prior content must be preserved.
'x' — Exclusive create
Fails if the file exists. Use when you must avoid overwriting any existing file.
Concrete example
To add a timestamped log entry without deleting prior entries, open the file in append mode. Using 'w' would replace the log each run.
Common mistake
Accidentally opening a persistent data file with 'w' instead of 'a' and losing historical data.

screens.title: Closing files and the with statement
screens.narratorSegment: Explicitly closing files by calling close is correct but fragile: if an exception interrupts your code before close runs, the operating system may keep the file handle open or buffered writes may not flush. The with statement creates a context manager. When you open a file using with open(...) as file, the context manager guarantees that close is called when the block ends, whether it completes normally or raises an error. This pattern avoids the common pitfall of forgotten close calls and is considered the Pythonic best practice for file handling. As a concrete comparison, consider writing a file and then raising an error inside the same block; with ensures the file is closed and buffers flushed, while manual close could be skipped. A helpful mental model: the with statement gives a safe, bracketed region where resources are live, and exiting the region always triggers cleanup. Use with for every file operation unless you have a compelling need for manual control, and then ensure finally blocks call close. The takeaway: prefer with to keep code robust and prevent resource leaks and partial writes.

keyIdea.title: Best practice

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › Context Managers
Process Flow

Using with for file safety

The with block creates a scope where the file is guaranteed to close when the block ends, even after exceptions.

# Bad practice
file = open("out.txt", "w")
file.write("Line one")
# If an error occurs here, file.close() might never run

# Good practice
with open("out.txt", "w") as file:
    file.write("Line one")
# File is closed automatically here
Use finally with manual close only when you have unusual lifetime needs; for typical I/O the with pattern is shorter and safer.
Concrete scenario

Imagine writing a log and then raising an exception. With ensures the log file is closed and the entry is flushed; without it you may lose recent writes.

Key Takeaway
Prefer with open(...) as file for all ordinary file operations to guarantee closure and flush behavior.

screens.title: Reading methods: read() explained
screens.narratorSegment: The read method returns the entire file content as a single string. It is convenient for small files or when you need the whole text in memory for operations like slicing or simple parsing. However, the memory cost grows with the file size. If the file is large, read can consume a lot of memory and slow your program or even cause it to run out of memory. A practical rule is to use read for small configuration files or short text files, and to prefer iteration or readline for larger datasets. For example, reading a configuration file into a string makes simple pattern searches easy, but reading a multi-hundred-megabyte log file with read is risky. A common misconception is that read is always simpler; it's simple, but not always safe. As a concrete example, the following code reads the whole file, prints a header, and shows the content. After this example we'll contrast read with line-by-line iteration, which is more memory-efficient for big files. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › read()

read() — all at once

Returns the entire content as a single string. Simple, but watch memory usage for large files.

with open("my_data.txt", "r") as file:
    content = file.read()
print("--- Full Content ---")
print(content)
When to use
Small files like short configs or templates.
When not to use
Large logs or datasets where memory could spike.
Concrete example
Read a small config file and split on newlines for simple parsing.

screens.title: Line-oriented reading: readline(), readlines(), and iteration
screens.narratorSegment: Python offers several line-oriented ways to read a file. readline reads a single line each call and returns it including the trailing newline. Repeated calls to readline progress the file pointer. readlines reads all lines into a list; it is convenient but, like read, loads the entire file into memory. The most memory-efficient and idiomatic way to process many lines is to iterate over the file object directly with a for loop. This yields one line at a time and keeps memory use minimal. A typical pattern is: open the file with a with statement, then for line in file: strip the newline, process the record, and perhaps write results elsewhere. A common misconception is that readlines is always safe; when the file is large, it can still cause memory issues. As a concrete illustration, we'll show three short snippets: one using readline in a loop, one using readlines to produce a list, and one iterating the file object. Practice the for line pattern for most file-processing tasks, and reserve readlines for small files where list semantics are useful. Line-oriented reading: readline(), readlines(), and iteration means iterate over the file object for memory-efficient line-by-line processing; use readlines only for small files.. In practical terms, how to process files line by line safely and efficiently. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › Line reading
Examples
# readline in a loop
with open("my_data.txt", "r") as f:
    line = f.readline()
    while line:
        print(line, end='')
        line = f.readline()

# readlines returns a list
with open("my_data.txt", "r") as f:
    lines = f.readlines()
    print(lines)

# iterate file object (most memory-efficient)
with open("my_data.txt", "r") as f:
    for line in f:
        print(line, end='')
Guidance
  • Prefer iteration for large files to keep memory usage low.
  • Use readline for controlled, manual progression when needed.
  • Use readlines only when you need random access to lines in memory.
Misconception
Iterating is slower than readlines — often false; iteration is both memory-efficient and simple, suitable for most tasks.

screens.title: Writing: write() and writelines()
screens.narratorSegment: The write method appends a single string to a file and does not add a newline automatically, so you must include '\n' where needed. writelines takes a list of strings and writes them sequentially; like write, writelines does not insert newlines for you. These behaviors are deliberate: they give you control over formatting. A common beginner mistake is assuming lines will be separated automatically and finding everything jammed together. If you have a list of names, ensure each entry ends with a newline before calling writelines. Also remember that write and writelines operate relative to the file pointer: when opened in append mode, writes go to the end; when opened in write mode, the file gets truncated first. Always open for writing inside a with block so the file is closed and buffers flush reliably after write operations. As a concrete example, we show writing three lines with write and writing a prepared list with writelines; both patterns are useful depending on how you prepare your output. In practical terms, how to write strings and lists of strings to text files. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › Writing

write() and writelines()

Both write text exactly as given. Add ' ' when you want new lines; prepare lists for writelines accordingly.

# Using write()
with open("out.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Hello, Cohortia!
")
    f.write("This is a new line.
")

# Using writelines() - ensure each element ends with a newline
lines = ["Alice
", "Bob
", "Charlie
"]
with open("out.txt", "w") as f:
    f.writelines(lines)
Concrete example
Prepare a list of uppercase names each ending with ' ' before calling writelines to write them cleanly.
Common mistake
Forgetting newlines and seeing concatenated output on a single line.

screens.title: Append vs Overwrite: choosing the right mode
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing append or overwrite affects whether existing file contents are preserved. Use append mode when each write is an incremental addition—log files typically use append so each run adds lines without erasing history. Overwrite mode ('w') is appropriate when you want a fresh file each run, for example when generating a new report. One risk is accidentally using 'w' on a persistent file and losing important data. Another useful mode is 'x' for exclusive creation: it fails if the file exists, which helps prevent accidental overwrites when you must ensure creation only happens once. In practice, think about intent: if you are adding entries over time, use 'a'; if you are replacing content intentionally, use 'w' and ensure you have backups if needed. Also consider atomicity: for critical files you might write to a temporary file and then rename it to avoid half-written states. For this chapter we emphasize correct mode selection and testing outputs by re-opening files to confirm content. In practical terms, decide whether to preserve existing data or replace it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Handling exceptions: FileNotFoundError and PermissionError
screens.narratorSegment: File operations can fail for predictable reasons. FileNotFoundError is raised when you try to open a file for reading that does not exist. PermissionError occurs when the program lacks rights to read or write the target path. The right approach is to wrap file access in try-except blocks for these cases. Use a try-except that first catches FileNotFoundError and informs the user or creates the missing file if appropriate. PermissionError should trigger a different response, such as notifying the user and aborting the write to avoid silent failures. For robust scripts, also include a broad except to log unexpected errors while still closing or cleaning up resources. When using the with statement, closure is guaranteed even if exceptions propagate. A concrete pattern is to try to open the file inside a try block and handle errors with clear messages. Common file exceptions and responses

FileNotFoundError
Raised when opening for read and the file is missing. Options: create a default file, surface a friendly error, or abort.
PermissionError
Raised when lacking permissions. Do not retry blindly; inform the user and suggest corrective actions.
try:
    with open("names.txt", "r") as infile:
        for line in infile:
            process(line)
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("Error: Input file not found.")
except PermissionError:
    print("Error: Insufficient permissions to access the file.")
except Exception as e:
    print(f"An unexpected error occurred: {e}")

Lab steps

Step 1 — Create input file
Write several names into names.txt, one per line for predictable input during testing.

# Starter template (adapt as needed)

    f.write("Alice
")

")

input_filename = "names.txt"
output_filename = "filtered_names.txt"
processed_names = []

try:
    with open(input_filename, 'r') as infile:
        for line in infile:
            name = line.strip()
            if len(name) >= 5:
                processed_names.append(name.upper() + '
')
except FileNotFoundError:
    print(f"Error: The file '{input_filename}' was not found.")

    with open(output_filename, 'w') as outfile:
        outfile.writelines(processed_names)

fullNarratorScript:
Files let a program keep data beyond a single run. In this lesson you will learn how Python opens files, how different file modes change behavior, and why closing files is important. We’ll practice reading methods that fit small and large files, and writing methods that let you create or append content. You will see the safe pattern using the with statement so resources are released even when errors occur. Practically, these skills let you save user settings, write logs, and process datasets stored as plain text. A common beginner mistake is choosing the wrong mode and unintentionally erasing data; we will highlight that risk and how to avoid it. By the end of the chapter you will be able to pick the right mode for a task, read files efficiently, write predictable output, and handle common file-related exceptions. Think of files as shared memory on disk: handled correctly they make programs durable, handled poorly they cause lost work. Ready to explore how open, read, write, and with work together?

These objectives describe concrete skills you will practice. First, you will understand file input and output fundamentals: what a file object is and why modes matter. This helps you avoid accidental data loss when writing. Second, you will learn to open and close files correctly, and to prefer the with statement so files are closed automatically even on errors. Third, you will master reading methods — reading the whole file, reading lines, and iterating — so you can pick memory-efficient patterns for large or small files. Fourth, you will write using write and writelines and handle common exceptions like FileNotFoundError and PermissionError. Each objective pairs a practical task with a reason: closing files prevents resource leaks, correct modes prevent overwrites, and appropriate read patterns avoid high memory use. Together these competencies let you build scripts that persist and transform plain-text data without losing information. At the end, you will verify results by reading outputs back and handling errors gracefully.

This second objectives screen focuses on practice: you will run small scripts that create, read, filter, and write text files. You'll practice creating a sample input file, then open it in read mode and iterate line by line so you can process large files without using excessive memory. You will filter names by length and write only the processed lines to a new file, ensuring each written line includes a newline. The practice also includes handling missing files with FileNotFoundError and catching unexpected errors to print helpful messages. These exercises teach both the A P I and discipline: always verify the mode you choose and confirm outputs by re-reading the written file. Finally, you will compare append and write modes by adding log entries and seeing how previous content is preserved or overwritten. Practicing these steps helps build intuition about when to use each method and how to avoid common mistakes.

When you call the open function you receive a file object: a Python handle that represents an interaction channel with disk storage. That object exposes methods like read, write, and close. Understanding that a file object is a resource explains why you must close it: the operating system allocates buffers and locks on your behalf, and those resources should be released when you’re done. A common misconception is that closing is optional because the interpreter will eventually clean up; while cleanup happens at program end, relying on it can lead to lost data or too many open handles in long-running programs. Use the file object to call read-based methods when you need input, or write-based methods to send text to disk. The file object also maintains the file pointer position; after reading or writing, subsequent operations continue from the pointer. Knowing this helps reason about why mixing read and write calls without adjusting the pointer can produce unexpected results. As a concrete example, opening a file in default mode returns a readable file object you can iterate over. The key takeaway: treat the file object as a resource you open, use, and reliably close.

File modes determine whether you can read, write, or append and whether a file is created or truncated. The default 'r' opens an existing file for reading and raises an error if it does not exist. 'w' opens for writing and will create a file if needed but will also truncate an existing file to zero length — this is why using 'w' when you intended to append causes accidental data loss. 'a' opens the file for appending: writes are added to the end and the file is created if missing, making it the safe choice for log entries. 'x' tries to create the file and fails with an exception if the file already exists; this is useful when you want exclusive creation. A common beginner mistake is using 'w' for repeated updates. For example, appending a log entry should use 'a', not 'w'. Another consideration is that modes can include a 'b' for binary; in this chapter we focus on text files, so use the default text mode. Always double-check the chosen mode to avoid losing content, and prefer explicit choices: if you need to preserve content, use 'a' or open and read-then-write with care.

Explicitly closing files by calling close is correct but fragile: if an exception interrupts your code before close runs, the operating system may keep the file handle open or buffered writes may not flush. The with statement creates a context manager. When you open a file using with open(...) as file, the context manager guarantees that close is called when the block ends, whether it completes normally or raises an error. This pattern avoids the common pitfall of forgotten close calls and is considered the Pythonic best practice for file handling. As a concrete comparison, consider writing a file and then raising an error inside the same block; with ensures the file is closed and buffers flushed, while manual close could be skipped. A helpful mental model: the with statement gives a safe, bracketed region where resources are live, and exiting the region always triggers cleanup. Use with for every file operation unless you have a compelling need for manual control, and then ensure finally blocks call close. The takeaway: prefer with to keep code robust and prevent resource leaks and partial writes.

The read method returns the entire file content as a single string. It is convenient for small files or when you need the whole text in memory for operations like slicing or simple parsing. However, the memory cost grows with the file size. If the file is large, read can consume a lot of memory and slow your program or even cause it to run out of memory. A practical rule is to use read for small configuration files or short text files, and to prefer iteration or readline for larger datasets. For example, reading a configuration file into a string makes simple pattern searches easy, but reading a multi-hundred-megabyte log file with read is risky. A common misconception is that read is always simpler; it's simple, but not always safe. As a concrete example, the following code reads the whole file, prints a header, and shows the content. After this example we'll contrast read with line-by-line iteration, which is more memory-efficient for big files. Python offers several line-oriented ways to read a file. readline reads a single line each call and returns it including the trailing newline. Repeated calls to readline progress the file pointer. readlines reads all lines into a list; it is convenient but, like read, loads the entire file into memory.
